question: What is the meaning of analysis of the demolition acquisition in relation to material layers, materials?
description: The analysis of the demolition acquisition in relation to material layers and materials involves assessing the different building elements and their corresponding masses. This analysis includes identifying specific building waste types, such as concrete demolition or construction waste, and mapping them to key-numbers for tracking purposes. Additionally, the analysis involves comparing the results of different assessment methods to determine the accuracy of the acquired data, considering factors like building components, material densities, and total masses of the building.

and the “waste material disposal certificate” was not possible. Still, it has 
to be stated that the aim of this paper is to test the transferability of the 
MP method, initially developed for new construction, on an existing 
building with regards to the material acquisition methods. Accordingly, 
the focus lies on the limitations and potentials of the material acquisition 
methods and not on the correctness of the acquired data. However, since 
the UMA is a very thorough assessment using destructive methods, the 
results are expected to be very accurate and correct. However, an 
assessment of the data uncertainties, which would help defining the 
reliability of the MP results, and a comparison with the actually disposed 
materials would be supportive, but were not conducted. 
5. Discussion 
This research has shown, that through the application of the MP- 
method, valuable results regarding the sustainability of buildings are 
generated. However, it has to be stated that the applied MP-method is a 
basic method, which should be refined and enriched with more influ­
encing parameters such as e.g. the deconstruction potential and location 
of a material within the building. The deconstruction potential could 
show how good two building components (e.g. a wall and a slab) can be 
separated from each other, without demolishing the components, thus 
enabling a higher reuse potential of the components. The location plays 
a crucial role, since it is more effortful to deconstruct a high-rise building 
than a single-storey building. A differentiation between the reuse and 
recycling potential should be conducted within the MP-method, since 
reuse of materials or elements requires less processing than recycling 
and therefore should be preferred at the deconstruction of the building. 
Moreover, the monetary value of the materials in existing buildings 
should be integrated into the MP assessments in order to enable a 
comparison of the prices of new and reused or recycled materials. Apart 
from that, using indicators from IBO might not always be correct, since 
this information is for new constructions and not for existing buildings. 
For the MP usually all the materials are included in the assessment, 
however it needs to be questioned, if this accuracy-level is necessary, 
since a detailed acquisition is an effortful and time-consuming process, 
as demonstrated within this work. Future research should address 
determining of the needed accuracy-level of the acquisition in the scope 
of a pre-demolition audit. Therefore, a clear description of the content of 
the MP for the end-of-life-phase is required. However, as shown in the 
results, in order to obtain correct results, it is necessary to either be very 
careful while acquisition or to compare the results with another acqui­
sition, since mistakes can occur easily. Apart from the fact that the 
acquisition is a very effortful process, to be conducted at the end-of-life 
stage of the building, it needs to be questioned if the existence of the MP 
in the pre-demolition phase has any value and if it helps to optimize the 
end-of-life phase of a material or element. It is obvious, that in the pre- 
demolition phase the state-of-the-art waste streams cannot be changed 
easily, due to the restricted time, which is why the MP should already be 
existing before the demolition-decision of a building. The existence of an 
MP in earlier stages, might enable the planning of the final stage of an 
element or material, thus might enable higher reuse or recycling rates. 
However, invasive methods, as applied within the UMA, can only be 
utilized, if the building is a demolition object.

3. Data assessment 
3.1. Challenges and potentials of the acquisition methods 
Laser scanning technology is a well-established method to conduct 
surveys on existing buildings. Within this research, some challenges 
occurred during data acquisition via laser scanning. Since the building 
was still occupied during the geometry acquisition, all occupants and 
furniture appeared in the point cloud (Fig. 3.), which appeared as clutter 
and therefore needed to be removed before the generation of the BIM- 
model. 
The results of the material survey through the DA and the UMA were 
compared regarding assessed masses and considered building elements. 
The DA was conducted within the scope of the pre-demolition audit, 
accordingly the results are mapped to “key-numbers”, which are linked 
to the type of waste. Each key-number represents a specific building 
waste type, whereby more than one material can belong to a building 
waste type. Each building waste type follows a certain disposal or 
recycling stream (e.g. transport to the processing plant for recycling, or 
specific disposal for dangerous materials). Within this use case some of 
the following demolition materials occurred: “Concrete demolition” 
with the key-number 31427-R, which was represented by bricks within 
this use case, whereby the “R” stands for recycling. Key-number 31409- 
D represents “construction waste” (e.g. aerated concrete within this use 
case), whereby the “D” stands for landfill. Key-number 31437-(g) stands 
for asbestos waste, whereby the “(g)” stand for “dangerous”. Fig. 4 
displays the results of the DA, structured regarding the type of waste. 
The UMA, as emerging field, did not follow any specific data struc­
ture. Thus, the results were depending on the building component 
(exterior walls, interior walls roof, etc.) and summed up regarding the 
most important materials within the construction sector (e.g. concrete, 
gypsum, mineral wool, etc.), as presented in Fig. 5. The different 
structure of the results required a restructuring in order to enable a 
comparison of the results. Throughout the comparison of the results 
some differences could be detected, such as the varying total mass of the 
building. The results of the DA showed a mass of 1.355 kg, whereas the 
assessed mass of the UMA was 1.882 kg. The difference was due to the 
wrong assumption of the share of reinforcement within the concrete 
foundation of the building within the UMA. Moreover, some assump­
tions about the densities did not comply within the material acquisition 
results. These results were adapted according to a mean value or by 
considering one of the proposed densities. The thickness of e.g. the 
bituminous sealing within the roof was assumed to be 1 cm in DA, which 
is the standard thickness for a sealing layer. However, within the UMA 
the thickness was determined as 2 cm. The thickness of the UMA was 
taken into consideration for follow up assessment, as it was based on a 
more precise method of cutting the roof to inspect each layer, which was 
omitted in the DA. 
After the adaptations of both acquisition results, still some differ­
ences occurred. These are due to the fact that the UMA was conducted 
more precisely and therefore included more building elements, which 
accordingly lead to a higher mass. E.g.: The total mass of concrete is 
1.046 kg according to DA, whereas the UMA identifies the total mass by 
1.112 kg. In total, the mass of the building, as acquired by the DA, is 
1.323 kg, whereas the mass acquired by the UMA is 1.456 kg. In both 
results concrete represents the largest share of all materials. The accu­
racy of assessment is also reflected in the acquisition time: for DA it was 
only 5 h, whereas for the UMA about 25 h. The comparison of the final 
results as well as the acquisition times of both assessment methods is 
shown in Table 1.
